questions.q: Describe Kafka in one sentence. What is a consumer's unit of progress?
questions.a: Kafka is a distributed, replicated, append-only commit log: the broker stores and serves the log, and the read position belongs to the consumer rather than to the broker. A consumer's unit of progress is an **offset** — one integer per partition, committed by its group. That single design decision is where every other property of Kafka comes from.

questions.q: Does a message disappear once it has been consumed? What actually decides when it is deleted?
questions.a: No. Reading is non-destructive — consuming only moves the group's offset forward. Deletion is driven entirely by the **retention policy** on the topic: by age (`retention.ms`), by size (`retention.bytes`), or by key for a compacted topic. A record nobody ever reads is deleted on schedule, and a record every group has read stays until retention says otherwise.

questions.q: Name two things a message queue gives you that Kafka does not.
questions.a: Per-message control — its own retry schedule, delay, priority, or dead-letter path — because the broker tracks state for every individual message. And broker-side routing: RabbitMQ exchanges can route by topic pattern or header, while a Kafka consumer reads a partition and filters for itself. Both follow from Kafka's broker holding no per-message state.

questions.q: Kafka vs RabbitMQ: give the selection criteria without comparing throughput.
questions.a: Compare the **unit of state**. Kafka tracks progress as a stream plus an offset — one number for a whole group. RabbitMQ tracks it per message: delivered, acked, requeued, retried how many times. So: if the problem needs control over individual messages, you are fighting Kafka's design. If it needs one event stream that several independent consumers share and can replay, you are fighting RabbitMQ's.

questions.q: Why does Kafka have no per-message retry, delay or priority? Tie it to the design rather than calling it a missing feature.
questions.a: Those features all require the broker to hold state per message and to hand records out in an order other than the one they were written in. Kafka's broker holds one offset per partition per group and serves a file sequentially — that is exactly why it can serve reads at near disk speed with page cache and zero-copy. Per-message semantics are not missing; they were traded away for that property.

questions.q: Adding a new downstream consumer six months after launch: what does that cost in Kafka, and what does it cost in RabbitMQ?
questions.a: In Kafka it is a new consumer group reading from offset 0 — it gets the full history still inside retention, and nobody already running is affected. In RabbitMQ the consumer list is decided at publish time: an exchange has to copy each message into one queue per consumer, so a queue bound today starts empty and everything published before it is gone. Adding a late consumer there is a producer change plus a backfill from somewhere else.

questions.q: When would you advise a team against Kafka? Give three concrete situations.
questions.a: **Low-latency request/reply** — Kafka is not RPC; a round trip through a log adds batching, replication and poll latency and gives you no correlation or timeout semantics. **Work needing per-task control** — its own retry, delay, priority or dead-letter path, especially with a worker count that swings; you would rebuild that machinery yourself. **Small scale, one consumer, no replay requirement** — the deciding cost is operational, not technical: a cluster to run, partition counts that cannot be undone, and someone who can diagnose a shrinking ISR at 2am. Three more worth having ready: fan-out to end clients, querying by message content, and scheduled delivery.

questions.q: How do Share Groups (KIP-932) differ from consumer groups, and what do they trade away?
questions.a: The difference everything else follows from is the **unit of distribution**: a consumer group distributes partitions, a share group distributes individual records. So many consumers can read one partition, parallelism is no longer capped by partition count, and progress becomes a per-record state machine — acquired → acknowledged / released / rejected, with a delivery count and an acquisition lock timeout — instead of one committed offset. The trade is usually stated as losing ordering, which is true but incomplete: **the broker now keeps state per in-flight record**, which is precisely what Kafka refused to do in order to stay fast. Share groups buy queue semantics by giving back the property that made the log cheap to serve.

questions.q: A team needs delayed delivery — "retry this in 30 minutes" — on Kafka. Design it, and state what you give up.
questions.a: The obvious design fails: you cannot publish to a delay topic and poll it checking timestamps, because a partition is a sequential log and a consumer cannot skip its head. A record due in 29 minutes blocks every record behind it — head-of-line blocking — and waiting inside the poll loop exceeds `max.poll.interval.ms`, so the consumer is evicted and the group rebalances. The working design is **tiered delay topics** (5s / 1m / 5m / 30m) so each topic holds a roughly uniform remaining wait, bounding the blocking to that tier's granularity; a consumer per tier reads the head, and when the record is not due it calls `pause()` on the partition and `seek()` back to that offset while continuing to `poll()` so heartbeats survive, then republishes to a smaller tier or the destination when due. Costs: ordering along the delay path, retention on every delay topic must exceed the longest delay or messages expire before firing, republishing is at-least-once so the terminal consumer must be idempotent, and precision is bounded by tier granularity. The simpler alternative, and usually the right one: a `due_at` column in a database plus a poller — "find the rows due now" is a query a database is built for and a log is not.

questions.q: Your company already runs RabbitMQ. A team wants to add Kafka for an event stream. Argue both sides of running two brokers.
questions.a: **For:** an event stream is a different problem from task dispatch. On a queue the consumer list is fixed at publish time, so a consumer added later sees no history; in Kafka it is a new group from offset 0 at no cost to anyone. Reprocessing after a bug becomes the same mechanism rather than a recovery project, and retention stops being a liability and becomes the feature. **Against:** two brokers is two sets of operational knowledge, two failure modes, two upgrade paths, two monitoring stacks and two runbooks — paid continuously by everyone, not once by the team that wanted it. Kafka's failure modes are also unfamiliar and subtle: ISR shrink, rebalance storms, lag that means something other than a slow consumer, a partition count that cannot be lowered. **The option usually left unexamined:** RabbitMQ Streams has existed since 3.9 — an append-only replicated log with consumer-controlled offsets and replay, with superstreams for partitioning — so the log semantics may already be running in production. Comparing Kafka against RabbitMQ *queues* answers the wrong question. **Decide with a test, not a preference:** add Kafka only when more than one independent consumer of the data exists today, replay is a stated requirement, the history itself has value, and somebody will own it operationally by name. If Streams covers the first three, the answer is no.
